meta.blurb: In 1665 a young Englishman put a flea, a needle and a slice of cork under a new microscope and drew what he saw. Open Hooke's famous book, and discover how much of the world is hidden in plain sight.
meta.bible: Robert Hooke: English scientist, born 1635 on the Isle of Wight, died 1703 in London; Curator of Experiments to the Royal Society from 1662; a clever instrument maker, draughtsman and thinker. Micrographia: his large book of drawings and notes, published in January 1665, dedicated to King Charles II, with about sixty Observations and many engraved plates, some folding out. Royal Society: the new London society of scientists, founded in 1660, which tested ideas by experiment. Samuel Pepys: the diarist who sat up until two in the morning reading it. Christopher Wren: Hooke's friend and the architect of the rebuilt London. Isaac Newton: the scientist with whom Hooke quarrelled. Antonie van Leeuwenhoek: the Dutch microscopist who found living creatures in water. Matthias Schleiden, Theodor Schwann: German scientists who, in the late 1830s, showed that living things are made of cells. London: where Hooke lived and worked; the Great Plague of 1665 and the Great Fire of 1666 struck the city. Key terms: Microscope, Telescope, Lens, Lenses, Cork, Cell, Cells, Needle, Razor, Flea, Louse, Gnat, Mould, Fossils, Crystals, Frost, Hygrometer, Oat, Mica, Muscovy glass, Petrified, Honeycomb, Armour, Saltpetre, Pulse, Pleiades, Drone-fly, Moon, Observations. Facts: the microscope magnified up to about thirty times and was lit by an oil lamp through a glass ball of water; Hooke counted more than a thousand million cells in a cubic inch of cork; his guess about the Moon's craters was wrong; no certain portrait of Hooke survives. Voice and tone: curious, exact and delighted, as if looking over Hooke's shoulder; where Hooke guessed or was mistaken, the text says so.

B1B2: In January 1665, a young London scientist named Robert Hooke published a large book called Micrographia. It was full of drawings of things so small that nobody had ever seen them clearly before.

Hooke was the Curator of Experiments for the Royal Society, a new group of curious men in London who wanted to test ideas by experiment. Every week he had to show them something new, and Micrographia grew out of that work.
In the preface, Hooke wrote that the human senses are weak and easily fooled. Instruments such as the microscope and the telescope, he said, could make them stronger and more honest.

Hooke's microscope was a tube of brass and leather with lenses inside, and it made small things look many times larger. He lit each specimen with an oil lamp, shining the light through a glass ball of water to make it brighter.
Hooke drew every specimen himself, looking at it again and again in different lights to be sure of its shape. Engravers then copied his drawings onto copper plates so that they could be printed.
Hooke began his book with the point of a needle, which looks perfectly sharp to the eye. Under the microscope it looked blunt and rough, full of bumps and scratches.
Next Hooke looked at a full stop printed in a book, which seems to the eye a neat and perfect round dot. Under the glass it was a ragged and uneven blot of ink.

Under the microscope, a razor looked like a rough ridge covered with scratches and grooves, although it seems perfectly smooth to the eye. Even the sharpest tools made by people, Hooke saw, are far from perfect when seen up close.

Hooke drew a lesson from these tests: the more closely we look at human work, the rougher it appears. But the works of nature, he said, often become more beautiful and more orderly the closer we look.

Hooke struck a flint against a piece of steel and caught the sparks on a sheet of white paper. Under the microscope, each spark was a tiny round ball of metal that had been melted by the heat of the blow.
Hooke believed that heat is not a substance but a very fast shaking of the tiny parts of a body. This idea was ahead of its time, and it fits well with what scientists think today.

One freezing morning Hooke looked at the frost on a window, and he found that it had grown into tiny feathers and ferns of ice. Each one was neatly shaped, as if an artist had drawn it with a very fine pen.
Hooke looked at crystals of salt and other minerals and noticed their sharp, regular shapes. He suggested that such shapes might come from piling up tiny round balls in neat heaps.

Hooke split a thin sheet of mica, then called Muscovy glass, into thinner and thinner plates. He found that a very thin plate shows bright colours, and that the colour depends on how thick the plate is.

To explain colours, Hooke suggested that light is a quick, shaking movement that spreads out like ripples on a pond. This was an early form of the wave theory of light, which later scientists developed.
Hooke looked at peacock feathers and found that their shining colours change as you turn them. He decided that the colours come from the fine structure of the feather, and not from paint or dye.
Hooke cut a slice of cork so thin that light could shine through it, using a very sharp penknife. He placed the slice under his microscope and looked carefully at what was inside.
The cork was made of tiny hollow boxes, packed together like the cells of a honeycomb. Hooke called them cells, and biologists still use that word for the building blocks of living things.
Hooke counted the cells along a short line, then worked out how many would fill a cubic inch. His answer was more than a thousand million, which shows how tiny they are.
Hooke also looked at the stems of living plants, such as elder and fennel, and found cells there too. In the fresh stems the cells were full of juice, while in the dead cork they held only air.
Hooke noticed a patch of blue mould growing on a piece of old leather. Under the microscope it was a forest of tiny stalks, each with a round head, like a field of small mushrooms.
Hooke studied the long bristle of a wild oat, which twists and untwists as the air becomes damp or dry. He suggested using it to measure moisture in the air, with a light pointer to show the changes.

Hooke looked at petrified wood, which looks and feels like stone, and found that it still shows the grain and tiny pores of real wood. He decided that it had once been living wood, slowly turned to stone by water.

Hooke turned to fossils such as shells found in rocks far from the sea. Many people thought they were tricks of nature, but he argued that they were the remains of animals that had once lived in water.
If fossils were the remains of living things, Hooke reasoned, they could be used like a record of the past. He thought that earthquakes had lifted old sea floors into hills and mountains.

Hooke asked why a fire burns, and he suggested that air contains a substance that dissolves burning things. He also believed that this same substance is found in saltpetre, which is used to make gunpowder.
After plants and rocks, Hooke turned to insects, and the microscope surprised him most of all. Tiny creatures that people usually crushed underfoot turned out to be built with astonishing care.
One of Hooke's best drawings shows a louse clinging to a single human hair with its hooked claws. Everyone knew this pest, but no one had ever looked at it so closely.
Hooke's drawing of the flea was so big that it had to be folded to fit in the book. Under the lens, the tiny jumper wore a suit of polished dark armour made of neat overlapping plates.
Hooke noticed that the flea's back legs were folded up like springs. When they suddenly straighten, he reasoned, they throw the insect many times its own length through the air.
Hooke watched the life of the gnat, which begins in the water as a wriggling larva. He saw it change shape, then split its skin and climb out as a flying gnat.
Hooke looked at the eye of a drone-fly and found that it is made of many thousands of tiny round lenses. He was amazed that such a small head could carry so many.
Hooke held the fly's eye toward a window and saw the window reflected in every one of the tiny lenses. It was like a crowd of little mirrors, each showing the same scene.
Hooke wondered how a fly can walk across a window or along a ceiling without falling. Under the microscope he found that each foot has two claws and soft pads, which seem to help it cling.
Hooke studied many other creatures, such as ants and spiders, and each one proved to be as intricate as the last. He drew the hairs on a leg and the jewelled colours of a wing with equal patience.
Looking at the thread of a silkworm, Hooke had a bold idea: perhaps people could make something like silk by artificial means. He suggested forcing a sticky liquid through tiny holes to form threads.
Hooke dropped balls into wet clay and saw round pits that looked like the craters on the Moon. But he decided that eruptions or bubbling were more likely than falling bodies, which was a mistake.
Hooke also looked at the stars through a long telescope. In the small group called the Pleiades he saw many dozens of stars, far more than the six or seven that the eye can find.

For Hooke, the microscope and the telescope were partners: one showed the very small, and the other the very far. Soon afterwards, a Dutchman named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek found tiny living creatures in a drop of water.
Hooke ended by hoping that better instruments and more careful eyes would uncover still more hidden things. He urged his fellow scientists to keep looking and to be honest about what they saw.
Micrographia was a big book, printed on large pages so that the drawings could be seen in detail. It contained about sixty observations, each with its own drawing or description.
In January 1665, Samuel Pepys, a busy official who kept a famous diary, bought a copy and began to read it. He sat up until two in the morning and called it the most ingenious book he had ever read.

The book was dedicated to King Charles II, and it made Hooke famous almost at once. Gentlemen all over England wanted microscopes of their own, so that they could look at the small world for themselves.
Plague struck London in 1665, and in 1666 a great fire destroyed much of the old city. Hooke, who was also a skilled surveyor, helped his friend Christopher Wren to plan the rebuilding.

Hooke was a restless inventor who made instruments and improved clocks. In 1678 he published the law of springs that still bears his name: the more you pull a spring, the longer it stretches, in proportion.
Hooke could be proud and quarrelsome, and in later years he argued with other scientists, including Isaac Newton. They disagreed about who had first thought of certain ideas about light and gravity.
Hooke died in London in 1703, after more than forty years of work for the Royal Society. Strangely, no certain portrait of him survives, so we cannot be sure what his face looked like.

In the late 1830s, two German scientists, Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann, showed that all plants and animals are made of cells. The name that Hooke gave to the empty boxes in cork had become the key word of biology.
Many of Hooke's ideas have been confirmed: light behaves as a wave, fossils were once alive, and fire needs air. Others, like his view of the Moon's craters, were mistaken.

Micrographia taught its first readers that the ordinary world becomes extraordinary as soon as we look at it with care. A needle, a flea, a slice of cork and a frosty window all became wonders in Hooke's hands.
C1C2: In January 1665, a young Englishman named Robert Hooke, then twenty-nine, published a large and handsome book called Micrographia, which opened a window onto a world that nobody had seen so clearly before. It was filled with engraved drawings of needles, insects, plants and crystals, all magnified until their hidden details stood out plain and strange. Within weeks it was the talk of London, and it remains one of the great books in the history of science.

Hooke served as the Curator of Experiments to the Royal Society, a new group of learned gentlemen in London who had agreed to test ideas by experiment instead of trusting old authorities. It was his duty to prepare something fresh and surprising for each weekly meeting, and the work required a very clever pair of hands. Much of Micrographia grew out of the demonstrations he gave there with his microscope, as he tried to astonish the members week after week.

In his preface, Hooke argued that the human senses are narrow and easily deceived, and that the mind is only as good as the evidence it receives. Instruments, he said, could widen what the senses reach, as the telescope had already done for the distant sky and as the microscope might now do for the very small. His great hope was that honest observation, patiently repeated, would slowly replace guesswork and old opinion.

Hooke's microscope was a tube of leather and brass with a lens at each end, and it could magnify an object up to about thirty times, which was a great marvel in that age. To light the specimen, he set an oil lamp beside it and placed a glass ball of water in between, so that the light was gathered into a bright spot. Even so, he had to struggle with dim light, blurred edges and tired eyes.

Hooke drew every specimen himself, looking at it again and again from different angles and in different lights, because he knew that a shadow can easily be mistaken for a shape. Engravers then copied his drawings onto copper plates, and the finest of them were printed on large sheets that folded out from the book. The plates were so carefully made that they remain a pleasure to look at, more than three and a half centuries later.

Hooke began his tour of the small with a humble sewing needle, whose point looks perfectly sharp to the naked eye. Under the lens, however, the point appeared blunt and rough, covered with bumps, scratches and ridges, like a poorly finished piece of iron. It was a first lesson in how much our eyes leave out, and it prepared the reader for many more surprises.

Next Hooke examined a full stop printed in a book, which seems to the eye a neat, round and perfectly black dot. Under the microscope it looked like an irregular and ragged blot of ink, with uneven edges and a rough surface. The most careful work of a printer, he showed, was far from perfect when seen up close.

A razor, which seems to the eye to have a perfectly smooth edge, looked under the microscope like a rough ridge cut with scratches and grooves. The cause was easy to understand, for the edge had been made by rubbing it on a stone, and the stone had left its marks. Hooke's point was that even the finest work of human hands is coarse when we examine it closely.

From these first tests Hooke drew a lesson that he would repeat throughout the book: the closer we look at things made by human hands, the rougher and less perfect they appear. The works of nature, on the other hand, usually grow more beautiful and more orderly with every increase in magnification. Nature, he suggested, is a craftsman with far finer tools than ours, and its smallest works are its most perfect.

To see what a spark really is, Hooke struck a piece of flint against steel and caught the sparks on a sheet of white paper. Under the microscope each of them proved to be a tiny round ball of metal, melted and made glowing hot by the force of the blow. It was a delightful discovery that the bright flash of a spark is made from a little piece of the steel itself.

Hooke concluded that heat is not a substance flowing from one body to another but a very rapid shaking of the tiny parts of which things are made. He pointed to the way a hard blow can make a metal glow, as it did when steel was struck by flint. It was a bold guess for 1665, and it agrees remarkably well with what scientists think today.

On a freezing morning, Hooke looked at the frost that had formed on a windowpane, and he found that it had grown into delicate ice feathers, leaves and ferns. Each one, he saw, was made of neat, regular shapes, and no artist could have drawn them more gracefully. It seemed to him that water, in freezing, has a hidden order of its own.

Hooke looked at crystals of salt and of other minerals under the microscope and noticed that their faces and angles are sharp and regular. He guessed that such shapes might come from the piling up of tiny round particles in neat heaps, as balls can be stacked in a regular pile. It was only a guess, but it was proved right in spirit more than two hundred years later, when scientists showed that crystals are built from atoms.

Hooke split a thin sheet of mica, a glassy mineral that people then called Muscovy glass, into thinner and thinner plates, and he looked at them in sunlight. A very thin plate, he found, shows beautiful colours, and the colour changes with the thickness of the plate. The same effect, he suggested, appears in other thin things, such as bubbles and films of oil.

To explain the colours, Hooke proposed that light is a very quick shaking or pulse that spreads outward from a bright body, much as ripples spread across a pond. This was one of the earliest forms of the wave theory of light, and later scientists developed it with great success. Hooke did not prove it, but he saw clearly that light needed an explanation of this kind.

In the feathers of a peacock, Hooke found shining colours that change as the feather is turned, from blue to green to gold. He decided that these colours do not come from paint or dye but from the fine structure of the feather itself, which he suspected was made of tiny, delicate layers. The explanation is close to what scientists believe today, and it was reached with nothing more than a lamp and a glass.

The best-known of Hooke's observations began with a piece of cork, a light and springy material that people used for stoppering bottles. With a penknife sharpened as keenly as a razor, he cut a slice so thin that light could pass through it, and he laid it under the lens. What he saw there was something that no one had ever described before, and it would change the study of life for ever.

The slice was filled with rows of tiny hollow boxes, pressed together like the cells of a honeycomb. The word cell was already used for the small rooms of a monastery, and Hooke chose it for these little chambers, a name that biologists still use for the building blocks of living things. Though he saw only the dead walls of plant cells, his word has lasted for more than three and a half centuries.

Hooke wanted to know how small the cells were, so he counted how many lay along a short line and used the result to work out how many would fill a cubic inch. His estimate came to more than a thousand million, a number so huge that it was hard for his readers to imagine. It was an early example of how a microscope can turn a guess into a measurement.

Hooke also examined the stems of living plants, such as elder and fennel, and found that they too were made of cells. In these fresh stems the cells were filled with juice, while in the dead cork they held only air. He was therefore close to understanding that plants are built from small units, though it would be a long time before anyone saw how important that fact was.

Hooke noticed a patch of blue mould growing on a piece of old leather, and he looked at it through the microscope with great curiosity. It was a forest of tiny stalks, each with a round head, rather like a field of small mushrooms. Mould, he concluded, is a kind of plant that can spring up wherever there is damp and decay.

Hooke studied the long bristle, or beard, of the wild oat, which twists and untwists as the air becomes damp or dry. He saw that this movement could be used to measure how moist the air is, and he suggested making an instrument from it, with a light pointer to show the changes. It is an early idea for what is now called a hygrometer, and it shows how closely Hooke looked at everything.

Hooke examined a piece of petrified wood, which looks like stone and feels like stone, and he cut a thin slice from it for the microscope. To his surprise, it still showed the grain and the tiny pores of real wood, just as an ordinary piece of oak or pine would. He decided that it must once have been living wood, soaked through by water carrying mineral that slowly turned it to stone.

Hooke then turned to fossils such as shells found in rocks far from the sea, which many people believed to be mere tricks of nature, shaped by some mysterious force inside the stone. He compared them with real shells and argued that they were the remains of animals that had once lived in the sea. That meant that places now far above the waves must once have been covered by water.

If fossils were the remains of living things, Hooke reasoned, then they were a kind of record, and a careful student might learn from them how the Earth had changed. He thought that earthquakes and other upheavals had lifted old sea floors into hills and mountains, burying many ancient creatures in the process. These were bold ideas for his day, and they made him one of the first to read the history of the Earth in its stones.

Hooke also asked why fire burns, and in his observation on charcoal he put forward a remarkable theory, namely that air contains a substance which dissolves burning things, and that this same substance is found in saltpetre. This would explain why a fire needs air to keep burning, and why saltpetre helps gunpowder burn even where there is no air. His idea was not quite right in detail, but it came very close to what we now know about oxygen.

After plants and minerals, Hooke turned to the insects, and here the microscope surprised him most of all. Tiny creatures that people usually swept away or crushed underfoot turned out to be built with astonishing care, with jointed armour, hairs, claws and eyes of extraordinary design. The more he looked, the more he felt that the smallest animal was as perfect a machine as any clock.

The louse, a pest that everyone knew and nobody admired, became one of Hooke's most striking drawings, in which it clings to a single human hair with its hooked claws. Its body is covered with bristles, and its short, strong legs end in grips designed for holding on tightly. Hooke seemed almost to admire the creature, which he described as remarkably well equipped for the way of life it had chosen.

His drawing of the flea, which unfolded to a great size from the page, became the most famous drawing in the book. Under the lens, the tiny jumper was clad in a suit of polished dark armour, made of overlapping plates and studded with sharp spines. Hooke thought it so handsomely jointed that he could not help admiring it, and he described it with the delight of a collector.

Hooke noticed that the flea's back legs were folded up like springs, which explained how such a small animal could leap so far. When the legs suddenly straighten, he reasoned, they throw the insect many times its own length through the air. It was a neat piece of engineering that no human maker could have matched.

Hooke also watched the life of the gnat, which begins in the water as a wriggling larva with a breathing tube at its tail. He saw the larva change into a different, curled form, and then split its skin so that a winged gnat came out and stood on the surface of the water. Few people had ever followed the whole story so closely, and the sight showed that even a tiny pest goes through remarkable changes.

The eyes of the drone-fly, a large fly that looks a little like a bee, were among the greatest wonders that he found. They are made up of a great many tiny curved surfaces, set closely together like the cells of a honeycomb, and Hooke counted them to be thousands, perhaps as many as fourteen thousand. He was astonished that so small a head could carry so many separate lenses, each one perfectly shaped for its work.

When Hooke held the eye toward a window, he found that every one of the little surfaces showed a tiny reflection of the same scene, like a crowd of miniature mirrors. He suspected that the fly sees the world through its many surfaces in a manner quite unlike our own. How a fly puts so many tiny views together was a mystery that he could not solve.

Hooke wondered how a fly can walk across a window or along a ceiling without falling, and he looked at its feet under the microscope. He found that each foot has two sharp claws for rough surfaces and soft, rounded pads that seem to help it grip smooth ones. The puzzle of how those pads really work was not fully answered until modern times.

Many other creatures passed under Hooke's glass in turn, including ants, spiders and mites, and each of them proved to be as intricate as the last. He drew the hairs on a leg, the jewelled colours of a wing and the bright eyes of a spider with equal patience. It seemed that wherever he looked, nature had left no part of its work unfinished.

Looking at the fine thread of the silkworm, Hooke had a bold idea: since silk is just a sticky liquid that dries into a thread, perhaps people could make something like it by artificial means. He suggested that a liquid might be forced through tiny holes to form threads, and then dried. It was more than two hundred years before the first artificial silk was made in this way.

Hooke turned his instruments to the Moon, and to find out how its round pits might have formed, he dropped balls into a mixture of clay and water and watched the hollows that appeared. He thought the Moon's pits were more likely made by bubbling or eruptions than by falling bodies, since he could not imagine where such bodies might have come from. Scientists now believe that most lunar craters were made by impacts, which shows how hard even the best guesses can be.

In the same book, Hooke looked at the stars through a long telescope, and he was struck by how many more of them appeared as his glass improved. In the little group called the Pleiades he saw many dozens of stars, far more than the six or seven that the naked eye can make out. He wondered whether any telescope, however powerful, would ever reach the end of them, and he left the question open for others.

For Hooke the microscope and the telescope were partners, one opening the world of the very small and the other the world of the very far. A few years later, a Dutch merchant named Antonie van Leeuwenhoek used single powerful lenses to discover living creatures too small to see in a drop of water. Between them, these instruments revealed that the universe of living things is far larger than the eye can show.

Hooke finished by hoping that better instruments and more careful eyes would uncover still more. He foresaw a time when people would use new tools to see things that were quite hidden in his day, and he urged his fellow scientists to keep trying. Honest observation, he thought, was the road to truth, and that road had hardly been begun.

Micrographia was a big book, printed on large pages so that the drawings could be seen in detail, and some of them folded out to several times the size of the page. It contained about sixty separate observations, each with its own drawing or description, from the point of a needle to the stars. A reader could open it almost anywhere and find something curious, and the pleasure of the book lay in turning the pages.

On a January evening in 1665, Samuel Pepys, a busy official who kept a famous diary, bought a copy of the book and began to read it. He was so delighted that he sat up until two in the morning, and he wrote that it was the most ingenious book that he had ever read in his life. Few scientific books have ever been given higher praise by an ordinary reader, and Hooke must have been delighted.

The book was dedicated to King Charles II, and it won Hooke a great reputation almost at once. Gentlemen and ladies all over England wanted microscopes of their own, so that they could look at the strange small world for themselves. Micrographia had made science fashionable, and it had shown that the new method of looking and drawing could be enjoyed by almost everyone.

In 1665, the year the book appeared, a terrible plague struck London, and in the year that followed, a great fire destroyed most of the old city. Hooke, who was also a skilled surveyor and designer, helped his friend Christopher Wren to plan the rebuilding, and he measured many of the new streets and plots himself. In that way, the man who had explored the world of the small also helped to shape a great city.

Hooke was a restless inventor, and Micrographia was only one of his many achievements. He designed instruments, improved clocks and springs, and in 1678 he published the law of springs that now bears his name, which says that the stretch of a spring grows in proportion to the force that pulls it. Engineers still use Hooke's law every day, from the design of bridges to the springs inside a watch.

Hooke could be proud and quarrelsome, and in his later years he argued bitterly with other scientists, among them the great Isaac Newton. They disagreed about who had been first to think of certain ideas about light and about gravity, and the quarrel did Hooke's reputation lasting harm. Historians today tend to see him as a brilliant but difficult man, whose merits were long underrated.

Hooke died in London in 1703, after a long illness, having worked for the Royal Society for more than forty years. Strangely, no certain portrait of him survives, so we cannot be sure what his face looked like, although his writing and his drawings speak for him very clearly. He left behind a large library and a great many ideas, and many of those ideas were taken up by others.

Hooke's cells, as they were first called, had to wait nearly two centuries for their true meaning to be understood. In the late 1830s, two German scientists, Matthias Schleiden and Theodor Schwann, showed that all plants and animals are made of cells, and that cells are the basic units of life. The name that Hooke gave to the empty boxes in a piece of cork had become the key word of modern biology.

Many of the ideas that Hooke sketched in Micrographia have been confirmed: light behaves as a wave in many ways, fossils are the remains of ancient life, and burning uses oxygen from the air. Others, like his view of the Moon's craters, were mistaken, and he would have been the first to say that the book was a beginning and not a final answer. That honest spirit, mixing bold guesses with careful looking, is what makes the book so valuable.

Micrographia taught its first readers a lesson that remains as fresh as ever, which is that the ordinary world becomes extraordinary as soon as we look at it with care. A needle, a flea, a slice of cork and a window of frost all became wonders in Hooke's hands, because he took the trouble to see them truly. Whoever has since peered into a microscope has followed the path that he opened in 1665.
